n: Abram leaves Egypt with his family and Lot and returns to the Negev in southern Canaan.

f.g: Travelers “go up” to Canaan’s higher ground and “go down” to Egypt.

n: Abram is now wealthy. In that culture, livestock and precious metals were the main forms of wealth. His riches will soon test his relationship with Lot.
Abram retraces his steps back to Bethel, where he had camped before going to Egypt. Returning to the place of the altar suggests spiritual renewal.
At the old altar Abram worships again, calling on the Lord’s name. After the troubles in Egypt, he comes back to where he first met God in the land.

f.w: called on the name of the LORD

n: Lot too has grown wealthy, with his own flocks, herds, and tents—he prospered by traveling with Abram.

f.g: Representing households and servants, not just shelters.

n: The land cannot support both of their large herds. Prosperity brings its own problems.
Their herdsmen quarrel over water and grazing land. The mention of Canaanites and Perizzites reminds us they were outsiders in a land already occupied—disunity was dangerous.

f.g: A people of the Canaanite hill country; the name may mean “village-dwellers.”

n: Abram, the elder, takes the lead in making peace. Family relationships matter more to him than winning an argument.
With great generosity, Abram lets Lot choose first. He trusts God to provide, whatever Lot picks.

f.g: Directions were often given facing east: left meant north, right meant south.

n: Lot looks out and sees the lush Jordan valley, as green as Eden or Egypt. The narrator’s aside—“before the LORD destroyed Sodom”—warns that looks can deceive.

f.g: The circle or valley of the Jordan near the Dead Sea.

n: Lot chooses the best-looking land and moves east. Once again, moving “east” in Genesis signals drifting from God’s presence.
Abram stays in Canaan, the land of promise, while Lot settles among the cities of the plain and moves his tent ever closer to Sodom.

f.g: Lot moves step by step toward Sodom; by 14:12 and 19:1 he lives inside the city.

n: The narrator bluntly warns that Sodom’s people were extremely wicked. Lot chose by appearances without weighing spiritual danger.

f.w: the men of Sodom were wicked

n: After Lot leaves, God speaks to Abram and tells him to look in every direction. Lot looked with his own eyes and chose; now God invites Abram to look and receive.

f.g: Echoes verse 10, where Lot “lifted up his eyes.”

n: God promises all the land Abram can see to him and his descendants forever. Abram’s generosity loses him nothing.
God also promises descendants as countless as the dust of the earth—an astonishing promise to a man with no children.

f.w: as the dust of the earth

n: God invites Abram to walk the land’s length and breadth, as an owner surveys property. Walking the land was a way of claiming it.

f.g: In the ancient world, walking over land could symbolize taking possession of it.

n: Abram settles by the great trees of Mamre near Hebron and builds another altar. Hebron becomes his main home and later the family burial place.

f.g: Better “the oaks (or terebinths) of Mamre,” named after an Amorite ally (14:13).
